parole.significato: to let go or pass, to admit to some place (to allow to get somewhere)
parole.testo: First attested at the end of the 12th century. A loanword from an Oghur Turkic language before the times of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin (at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries). Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *boĺo- (“to free, liberate”) which is a derivation from the adjective *

parole.significato: badger, brock common name for European badger, Eurasian badger (Meles meles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from a Turkic language. Compare Karakhanid بُرْسْمُكْ (borsmuk), Chagatai بورسوق (borsuq), Turkish porsuk, Azerbaijani porsuq, Kazakh борсық (borsıq), Bashkir борһыҡ (borhıq), Uyghur بورسۇق (borsuq) and Chuvash пурӑш (purăš). Ultimately, from Proto-Turkic *borsuk (“badger”).

Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *boĺ (“empty, free”). Its meaning developed from the original “exemption” in two ways: * permission to leave → bidding farewell → farewell, and * absolution, remission → pilgrimage for this goal → commemoration → the feast on this occasion.

First attested in 1800. Encountered first in science writers, considered mediated by a transcription in scientific literature such as tsitskan or Zyzkan of a descendant of Proto-Turkic *sïčgan (“mouse”), but also close to Romanian chițcan (“shrew”). With Hungarian ending in analogy to other words li

From csökik (“to decrease”, a dialectal verb from Proto-Turkic *čök-, compare Ottoman Turkish چوكمك (çökmek)) + -evény. Created during the Hungarian language reform, which took place in the 18th–19th centuries. Compare Hungarian csökött and csökken.
From the dialectal csökik (“to subside, decrease”, from Proto-Turkic *čök-, compare Ottoman Turkish چوكمك (çökmek)) + -en (instantaneous suffix). Compare Hungarian csökött and csökevény.

parole.significato: to topple, to tumble (optionally with lative suffixes)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tüĺ- (“to fall, move down”).

parole.significato: cattail (any of several perennial herbs, of the genus Typha, that have long flat leaves, and grow in marshy places)
parole.testo: From a Chuvash type Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *yẹgen (“rush”).

Connections with Proto-Turkic *koŋrak (“bell”) or *kaŕgan (“cauldron”) (see Bashkir ҡыңғырау (qıñğıraw) and Turkish kazan respectively) are usually proposed, however neither etymology is without problems.

parole.significato: arm (upper limb of a human or animal)
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *karï (“forearm”) via Bulgar, compare Chuvash хур (hur, “span”).
Variant of kolokán (“water soldier, Stratiotes aloides”), itself of Turkish origin, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kara (“black”).

Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kičin. Borrowed from a Chuvash-like Turkic language before the times of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin (at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries). Compare Chuvash кӗҫӗн (kĕś̬ĕn).
From Proto-Turkic *kopuŕ, through voiced (p>b) Kipchak-Cuman kobuz.

parole.significato: hound (a small to medium-sized hunting dog with strong legs, drooping ears, and a relatively short, pointed tail)
parole.testo: From the kop variant of kap (“to seize, grab”) + -ó (present-participle suffix). The figurative sense developed metaphorically based on the original sense. First attested in c. 1422 Alternatively, from Proto-Turkic *köpek (“dog”), for which compare Russian кобе́ль (kobélʹ, “male dog”).
Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *kȫĺek (“young of camel”), compare Turkish köşek (“young camel”), Mongolian гөлөг (gölög, “puppy”).

Controversial origin: * From Bulgar (Oghur Turkic) *nyār, from Proto-Turkic *yāŕ (“spring, summer”). Compare Chuvash ҫур (śur, “spring”), and (from common-Turkic *jāz) Yakut саас (saas, “spring”), Tuvan час (ças, “spring”), Kazakh жаз (jaz, “summer”), Old Turkic 𐰕𐰖 (y¹z, “summer”), Turkish yaz (“sum
Possibly from Proto-Turkic *ogrï (“thief”).
From Proto-Turkic *sakal. Compare Turkish sakal, Crimean Tatar saqal.

parole.significato: Tarján (one of the seven Hungarian tribes before and during the conquest of the Carpathian Basin)
parole.testo: From a Turkic language, compare Proto-Turkic *tarkan (“feudal or regional lord”).
From Proto-Turkic *turma (“radish”). Compare Turkish turp (“radish”), Persian ترب (torob, “radish”).

parole.significato: A Slovak (less commonly, Slovene) person, or a person of such origins.
parole.testo: Ultimately from Proto-Turkic *tāt (“alien, stranger, pagan”). Alternatively from Gothic "thuat", a Gepid tribal name. Possible cognates with German Deutsch and English Dutch, Teuton.

parole.significato: Turkish (of, from, or relating to Turkey, its people or language)
parole.testo: From Old Hungarian Turcu (türkü), from Proto-Turkic *tür(ü)k (see there for more). Borrowed before the times of the Hungarian conquest of the Carpathian Basin (at the turn of the 9th and 10th centuries).
From a descendant of Proto-Turkic *teŕek (“dung”) akin to Ottoman Turkish تزك (tezek).

First attested in 1222 as a place name in Regestrum Varadinense. Borrowed from an Oghur Turkic language, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *ïgač (“tree; wood”). Compare Turkish ağaç (“tree”), Turkmen agaççy (“carpenter”), Uyghur ياغاچچى (yaghachchi, “carpenter”), Salar [Term?] (“carpenter”).
From an unattested stem + -öl. Alternatively, suggested to be a Turkic borrowing from Proto-Turkic *yǖl- (“to be mad, crazy; anger; to be sexually excited”).

Likely from Oghur, from Proto-Turkic *koŋur; compare Chuvash хӑмӑр (hămăr). Alternatively, from an otherwise unattested stem of unknown origin + -r (nominal-forming suffix). It is also possible that it is a back-formation from komorodik or komorul.

Inherited from Old Hungarian ollo, ollow (“kid (of a goat)”), which is borrowed from Danube Bulgar *oɣloŭ, ultimately from Proto-Turkic *oɣul-aɣ (“young of an animal”). The modern sense of "scissors" is apparently because scissor blades swing like a goat's legs. Alternatively, from obsolete sense "r

parole.significato: interpreter (one who listens to a speaker in one language and relates that utterance to the audience in a different lan…
parole.testo: Borrowed either directly from Turkic, from Proto-Turkic *tilmaç (“interpreter”) – Chuvash тӑлмач (tălmač, “interpreter”) –, or via a Slavic language, Proto-Slavic *tъlmačь (“interpreter”).
